n:
- Artaxerxes I ruled Persia from 465 to 424 BC. 

- The fortress of Susa served as the Persian king’s winter palace.

In Nehemiah’s time, many Jews had already moved back to the land of Judah. They moved back from Babylon where they had been forced to live in exile.

They were back in the land God had given to the family line of Abraham. But the people of Israel were no longer in charge. They weren’t the rulers of the northern kingdom or the southern kingdom. The entire land of Israel was controlled by the government of Persia.

The Jews who moved back built a new temple. This showed that they were God’s people and worshipped only God. This was part of living as a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.

Yet the wall of Jerusalem was still broken down. This showed that they were no longer a strong nation. They weren’t strong like when David and Solomon were kings. The broken wall was a sign of the judgement God brought against his people.

They hadn’t been faithful to the Mount Sinai covenant. So they faced the covenant curses. Nehemiah’s prayer showed that he understood this. In his deep sadness, Nehemiah went without food. This is called fasting. He prayed constantly and admitted to God how the Israelites had sinned.

All of God’s people had done evil things. Nehemiah recognised that this included himself and his family. In his prayer Nehemiah remembered things that were true about God. God is always faithful to his covenant. Nehemiah asked God to keep his promises to his people. God’s people took delight in bringing honour to God’s name. Yet the broken wall of Jerusalem brought them shame. So Nehemiah made careful plans to rebuild the wall. He asked God to give him success when he told Artaxerxes his plans.

When Nehemiah heard about Jerusalem's ruins, he prayed for God's help ({{Nehemiah 1:1-11|Nehemiah 1:1–11}}) and asked the king to send him to Jerusalem ({{Nehemiah 2:1-8|2:1–8}}). Upon arrival, he urged the people to rebuild the city's wall ({{Nehemiah 2:11-20|Nehemiah 2:11–20}}).

- Hanani might have been one of Nehemiah’s actual brothers. In Hebrew, this word can also mean a fellow countryman (for example, {{Deuteronomy 1:16|Deuteronomy 1:16}}). 

- *the remnant of the Jews who had survived the exile*: See {{Ezra 2:64-65|Ezra 2:64–65}}; {{Ezra 8:1-14|8:1–14}}.

- *The wall of Jerusalem is broken down*: This likely refers to a recent event in Jerusalem (see {{Ezra 4:6-23|Ezra 4:6–23}}), not the Babylonian conquest in 586 BC. 

- disgrace: Foreigners could mock the destroyed city, claiming it showed that Israel’s God was too weak to protect it (compare {{Joel 2:17|Joel 2:17}}; {{Micah 7:8-10|Micah 7:8–10}}).
Nehemiah mourned, fasted, and prayed for about four months (compare {{Nehemiah 1:1|Nehemiah 1:1}}; {{Nehemiah 2:1|2:1}}), deeply worried about Jerusalem.

Nehemiah’s prayer includes: 

- Praise ({{Nehemiah 1:5|Nehemiah 1:5}})

- Confession ({{Nehemiah 1:6-7|Nehemiah 1:6–7}})

- Remembering God’s promises ({{Nehemiah 1:8-9|Nehemiah 1:8–9}})

- A request ({{Nehemiah 1:10-11|Nehemiah 1:10–11}})

Nehemiah understood that Israel’s situation was not due to God failing His covenant of unfailing love. Instead, Israel’s ongoing sin led to the punishments described in the covenant.

*I confess the sins that we Israelites have committed*: Like Ezra ({{Ezra 9:5-15|Ezra 9:5–15}}) and Daniel ({{Daniel 9:4-19|Daniel 9:4–19}}), Nehemiah identified with his people's sins. He made no excuses and accepted his own responsibility and that of the larger covenant group that had sinned against God.

- Nehemiah remembers God's curse on sin and his promise to restore ({{Deuteronomy 4:25-31|Deuteronomy 4:25–31}}; {{Deuteronomy 30:1-5|30:1–5}}). 

- *The place...for My Name *was Jerusalem.
Nehemiah refers to God's long-standing covenant with the Israelites. God rescued them during the exodus ({{Deuteronomy 9:29|Deuteronomy 9:29}}) and made them his servants.

- *grant him mercy in the sight of this man*: Nehemiah knew God could make the king kind to him. 

- As a cup-bearer, Nehemiah tasted the king’s wine to ensure it was safe. This role gave him daily access to King Artaxerxes.
*never been sad in his presence*: A servant should not let personal issues affect serving the king.

Nehemiah was a faithful and trusted worker in the Persian government in Susa. This was in keeping with Jeremiah’s advice to the Jews who lived in exile. They were to work for the success of the city God sent them to (Jeremiah 29:7).

The king was pleased with Nehemiah’s work. This helped Nehemiah have success when he made his request to Artaxerxes. God also helped Nehemiah have success when he talked with Artaxerxes. The king allowed Nehemiah to travel to Jerusalem to rebuild the walls of the city. Artaxerxes provided everything Nehemiah needed to accomplish the task.

The Jews in Jerusalem didn’t know Nehemiah’s plans. First Nehemiah explained how much God used Artaxerxes to help him. Then the Jews were ready to join him in the work.

Some people opposed the work of rebuilding the wall. This included Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem. They were officials from other people groups who lived in and around Jerusalem. They falsely accused Nehemiah. They said that Nehemiah was going against the authority of the Persian government. They said this because the wall would help Jerusalem be a strong military fort. It would help protect the people inside from being attacked.

But Nehemiah’s desire to rebuild the wall came from God. It wasn’t based on wanting to have power for himself and to fight against Artaxerxes. Nehemiah didn’t want those officials to be part of the community in Jerusalem. He didn’t want them to be part of the worship practices in the temple. The reasons for this are explained in other stories about them (Nehemiah chapters 4 and 6). They were outsiders who wanted to control Jerusalem and the Jews.

Outsiders who were completely committed to the Lord could be part of the community of God’s people. But outsiders who didn’t respect God, his commands or his people weren’t welcome.

Nehemiah felt scared because he showed his sadness and did not know how the king would react if he explained why he was upset. King Artaxerxes had earlier ordered that Jerusalem should not be rebuilt ({{Ezra 4:21-22|Ezra 4:21–22}}). Nehemiah was not pretending; his deep mourning was visible despite his efforts to hide it.
Nehemiah showed his loyalty by saying, *May the king live forever!* (compare {{Daniel 2:4|Daniel 2:4}}), but he still admitted his sadness.
*What is your request?*: The king followed the God of heaven, and Nehemiah needed God's guidance and help for his request.

*send me to Judah...so that I may rebuild it*: Artaxerxes’ willingness to consider this proposal is surprising given Jerusalem’s history of rebellions against Persia ({{Ezra 4:17-23|Ezra 4:17–23}}). The king might have seen Nehemiah’s plan as a way to strengthen his control over a problematic area of his empire.
*How long will your journey take* (see {{Nehemiah 5:14|Ezra 5:14}}): Nehemiah likely asked for a short time at first and later requested more time.

- Temple fortress might mean the Tower of Hananel or the Tower of the Hundred. 

- *the gracious hand of my God was upon me*: Nehemiah understood that God guided the king to grant these requests.
Nehemiah was a government official, so officers and horsemen escorted him to Jerusalem (compare {{Ezra 8:22|Ezra 8:22}}).

- Some local non-Jewish officials were unhappy because rebuilding Jerusalem's walls would shift political power to the Jews. 

- Sanballat led the opposition to Nehemiah's rebuilding efforts. 

- *the Horonite*: He was likely from Upper or Lower Horon (Beth-horon, {{Joshua 16:3|Joshua 16:3}}), about 19 kilometers (12 miles) northwest of Jerusalem. Sanballat's name suggests he might have descended from the Assyrians brought by Sargon II after Samaria's fall ({{2 Kings 17:24|2 Kings 17:24}}). A document found in Egypt shows he became Samaria's governor in 408 BC.

Nehemiah needed to see the walls himself to make strong plans for rebuilding and to gather the workers he needed. He secretly checked the walls at night to avoid being seen by his enemies. He only inspected the southern part of the city.

- Jackal’s Well might have been En-rogel, a water source about 365 meters (400 yards) south of the city, or the Pool of Siloam, which fills with water from Hezekiah’s winding tunnel. 

- The Dung Gate, called *the Potsherd Gate* in {{Jeremiah 19:2|Jeremiah 19:2}}, is at the southern end of the western wall (see {{Nehemiah 3:13|Nehemiah 3:13}}) and led to the Hinnom Valley, where city inhabitants threw their garbage.
The King’s Pool was likely the Pool of Siloam or another pool southeast of the city. Both pools were made from the overflow of the Gihon Spring (see {{2 Kings 20:20|2 Kings 20:20}}).

- Nehemiah kept his inspection and rebuilding plans secret from both the Persian and Jewish leaders to prevent organized opposition. Now, Nehemiah was ready to lead the rebuilding effort. 

- *the trouble we are in*: The broken walls brought disgrace to the city and reflected poorly on God. Jerusalem certainly did not resemble *the city of the great King* ({{Psalm 48:2|Psalm 48:2}}).

Clear evidence of God's involvement ({{Nehemiah 2:8|Nehemiah 2:8}}) strongly motivates any project. Nehemiah had God's guidance, the king's permission, the letters needed to get lumber, and a plan to lead the project. As a result, the people eagerly agreed to start working.

- Nehemiah’s enemies quickly mocked and tried to halt progress. These opponents were dangerous because they could discourage the people and damage Nehemiah’s credibility. 

- *Are you rebelling against the king?*: This serious accusation could lead to death (see also {{Ezra 4:6-23|Ezra 4:6–23}}).
The title *God of heaven* showed Persian audiences that Israel's true God was not just a local god. Nehemiah focused on obeying his ruler by building the walls.

- Eliashib, the high priest and grandson of Jeshua ({{Nehemiah 12:10|Nehemiah 12:10}}), led the priests in repairing the northern wall around the temple. 

- The Sheep Gate was where people brought sheep for sacrifice at the temple. 

- The Tower of the Hundred and the Tower of Hananel were two major military towers along the northern wall ({{Nehemiah 12:39|Nehemiah 12:39}}; {{Jeremiah 31:38|Jeremiah 31:38}}; {{Zechariah 14:10|Zechariah 14:10}}).
Eight work groups rebuilt the walls and gates in the city's northern section.
This summary describes the people who rebuilt Jerusalem's walls. It moves in a circle around the city, starting at the northeast corner, then going west, south, east, and north.

Jewish men and women from many towns and cities helped rebuild the wall. So did priests, leaders, traders, people who worked with gold and people who made perfume. Temple servants helped as well. They had a clear plan.

All together they worked very hard for the same goal. They finished building the wall in 52 days. They faced many problems as they worked. Some of the problems came from the people groups around them. These groups were willing to kill the Jews to stop them from building the wall. These groups also tried to harm Nehemiah. Nehemiah made clever plans to protect the people while they kept working. And he had complete trust in God’s power to protect them.

Some of the problems came from within the Jewish community. Some Jewish nobles didn’t help rebuild the wall. They worked against Nehemiah to stop the work. A priest and many prophets tried to make him afraid of being attacked. And there were nobles and officials who took advantage of needy people. These leaders weren’t following God’s example of how to be rulers.

Nehemiah did follow God’s example. He used his authority as governor to do what was good for the Jewish people. He corrected the problems so that the needy people were taken care of. He didn’t try to get rich by making people give him money. Instead, he provided what other people needed. He used the food and supplies the Persian government gave him to do this. He made sure that honest leaders who respected God were in charge in Jerusalem.
At the Fish Gate, people sold fish from the Sea of Galilee and the Mediterranean Sea.

- *Meremoth*: See {{Ezra 8:33|Ezra 8:33}}. 

- Meshullam married his daughter to Tobiah's son ({{Nehemiah 6:18|Nehemiah 6:18}}; see also {{Nehemiah 10:20|10:20}}).
Geshem, who controlled the area south of Tekoa, might have influenced Tekoa's leaders ({{Nehemiah 2:19|Nehemiah 2:19}}).
*The Jeshanah Gate*: The oldest part of Jerusalem was on an eastern hill that extended north to the Temple Mount.
These verses describe the work on the walls and gates on the western side of Jerusalem. People from outside the city and those with wealth or delicate jobs also helped.
Gibeon and Mizpah are about ten kilometers (six miles) north of Jerusalem.
The Broad Wall stood in the newer, western part of the city.
Nehemiah wisely assigned people to work near their homes. This motivated them to do good work and saved them travel time.
The Tower of the Ovens on the city's western wall might have been used for baking bread or polishing pottery ({{Jeremiah 19:1-2|Jeremiah 19:1–2}}).
Zanoah was a village located about 21 kilometers (13 miles) southwest of Jerusalem.
The Beth-haccherem district could have been about 3.2 kilometers (two miles) south of Jerusalem, at what is now Ramat Rachel, or eight kilometers (five miles) west, at what is now Ain Karem.
These verses focus on rebuilding the southern tip of the city where the Hinnom Valley and Kidron Valley meet.

- The Mizpah district was about ten kilometers (six miles) north of Jerusalem. 

- The king’s garden was a lush area east of the pool of Siloam. It was near the meeting point of the Kidron and Hinnom Valleys, possibly at the King’s Pool ({{Nehemiah 2:14|Nehemiah 2:14}}).

- The district of Beth-zur was just north of Hebron. 

- The tombs of David’s family might refer to where King David was buried ({{1 Kings 2:10|1 Kings 2:10}}; {{1 Kings 11:43|11:43}}; {{2 Chronicles 21:20|2 Chronicles 21:20}}; {{Acts 2:29|Acts 2:29}}). The House of the Mighty might have been a tomb for David’s mighty men ({{2 Samuel 23:8-39|2 Samuel 23:8–39}}).
These verses describe how they built the new eastern wall.
The angle and the corner refer to an unknown bend in the wall.
The tower rising from the king’s upper house and the court of the guard likely refers to a royal complex on Ophel Hill, just south of the temple area.

- This final group of workers completed the repairs at the Sheep Gate, where the work had begun ({{Nehemiah 3:1|Nehemiah 3:1}}). 

- *Horse Gate*: See {{2 Chronicles 23:15|2 Chronicles 23:15}}; {{Jeremiah 31:40|Jeremiah 31:40}}. 

- *East Gate*: See {{1 Chronicles 26:14|1 Chronicles 26:14}}, {{1 Chronicles 26:17|17}}; {{2 Chronicles 31:14|2 Chronicles 31:14}}; {{Ezekiel 10:19|Ezekiel 10:19}}; {{Ezekiel 40:21-22|40:21–22}}.

- The Persians placed Samarian army officers in Jerusalem to maintain peace. 

- *feeble Jews*: Sanballat's mockery had some truth. The Jews were not wealthy, powerful, or numerous. However, Sanballat did not understand the strength of the God the Jews served. 

- *Can they restore...Will they offer sacrifices?*: Sanballat might have mocked the sudden increase in sacrifices at the temple as the Israelites dedicated their work to the Lord. 

- *burnt stones...mounds of rubble*: When fire destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC, it heated the stones, causing some to crack and crumble. The people used these stones to rebuild the walls.

Nehemiah prayed intensely for God to stop those who opposed God's will. Nehemiah often called out to God when he needed help ({{Nehemiah 2:4|Nehemiah 2:4}}; {{Nehemiah 5:19|5:19}}; {{Nehemiah 6:14|6:14}}; {{Nehemiah 13:14|13:14}}, {{Nehemiah 13:22|22}}, {{Nehemiah 13:29|29}}, {{Nehemiah 13:31|31}}).
*Do not...let their sin be blotted out from Your sight*: See also “Prayers for Vengeance” Theme Note.
*half its height*: The wall might be 3.0 to 3.7 meters (ten to 12 feet) tall. Some scholars think the original wall was six to 7.3 meters (20 to 24 feet) high.

Enemies of Israel from the north (Sanballat), south (Arabs), east (Ammonites), and west (Ashdodites) were angry about Jerusalem's fast and successful rebuilding. This progress threatened their political power in the area.
*we prayed...and posted a guard*: This wise approach to the threat involved both trusting in God and taking necessary actions.
The constant psychological attacks from Israel's enemies were lowering morale.
*Wherever you turn, they will attack us*: Jews from nearby areas might have urged the people working in Jerusalem to return to their villages to avoid being killed in an attack.
Nehemiah responded by placing armed guards at the weakest parts of the wall. He ensured that opponents outside could see the forces ready to defend the city.

The greatest reason for hope was Israel’s powerful and glorious God, who had saved them from strong nations before (compare {{2 Chronicles 32:7-8|2 Chronicles 32:7–8}}; {{Exodus 14:13-14|Exodus 14:13–14}}; {{Deuteronomy 8:1-3|Deuteronomy 8:1–3}}; {{Deuteronomy 20:3|20:3}}; {{Joshua 10:25|Joshua 10:25}}). Another reason was to protect their families and properties.

Nehemiah credited God (see also {{Nehemiah 2:20|Nehemiah 2:20}}; {{Nehemiah 6:16|6:16}}). God had thwarted them through the people's prayers, the 24-hour patrol, the visible show of force, and confidence in God's protection.
Nehemiah used the trumpeter to sound the alarm and direct workers to any part of the wall under attack.

*Our God will fight for us!*: Nehemiah used Israel’s ancient holy war tradition ({{Exodus 14:14|Exodus 14:14}}; {{Deuteronomy 1:30|Deuteronomy 1:30}}; {{Deuteronomy 20:4|20:4}}; {{Joshua 10:14|Joshua 10:14}}; {{Joshua 23:10|23:10}}) to assure the people that they would win if they trusted in the Lord.
Nehemiah and the other leaders were not elitists who rested while others worked hard.
Severe financial problems almost stopped the wall's completion ({{Nehemiah 5:1-5|Nehemiah 5:1–5}}), but Nehemiah found a solution ({{Nehemiah 5:6-13|5:6–13}}).

Some farmers stopped growing crops to help build the wall. This left their large families needing food. Someone had to feed their families, or the farmers would stop working on the wall and return to their fields.
Some small landowners had mortgaged everything to survive. The famine worsened the problem because grain was scarce and food prices naturally rose.
*pay the king’s tax*: Despite the famine, the Persians did not cancel the heavy royal taxes due at harvest time.
*we are subjecting our sons and daughters to slavery*: See {{Exodus 21:1-11|Exodus 21:1–11}}. These families were desperate.
Nehemiah was very angry, but he controlled himself. He thought it over and then spoke to resolve the conflict instead of worsening it (see {{James 1:19-20|James 1:19–20}}).

- *walk in the fear of our God*: See {{Leviticus 25:35-43|Leviticus 25:35–43}}. 

- *avoid the reproach*: See also {{Nehemiah 1:3|Nehemiah 1:3}}; {{Nehemiah 2:19|2:19}}; {{Nehemiah 4:1-3|4:1–3}}.

*I...have been lending*: Nehemiah and his associates made loans without burdening people. Nehemiah’s example was to give financial help without causing more debt by charging interest (see {{Deuteronomy 15:7-11|Deuteronomy 15:7–11}}).

Nehemiah demanded that the wealthy lenders return the fields and repay the interest (literally *the hundredth part*), which they should not have collected (see also {{Exodus 22:25|Exodus 22:25}}; {{Leviticus 25:35-37|Leviticus 25:35–37}}). The term *hundredth part* suggests the interest was one percent per month. This was lower than the 20 percent annual rate found in some documents of that time, or the 60 percent annual rate charged at Elephantine in Egypt. However, even a low interest rate violated God's covenant.
*required of the nobles and officials an oath*: Both God and the community would hold them accountable.

- This is the first time Nehemiah is mentioned as governor. The king did not mention this role when he first sent Nehemiah to Jerusalem. 

- Persia's government officials usually received an official food allowance from the local population. However, Nehemiah and his associates bought food with their regular pay instead.
This section explains Nehemiah's steady approach to servant leadership and his personal generosity.

The former governors were likely Nehemiah’s immediate predecessors, not Sheshbazzar ({{Ezra 1:8|Ezra 1:8}}, around 90 years earlier) or Zerubbabel ({{Haggai 1:1|Haggai 1:1}}, around 80 years earlier).
Nehemiah prayed for God to remember and bless him, showing his reliance on God.
After solving the financial crisis (see {{Nehemiah 5:1-19|Nehemiah 5}}), the story shifts back to how those against rebuilding tried to scare or stop Nehemiah.
The plain of Ono, located near Lod ({{Ezra 2:33|Ezra 2:33}}), was likely a neutral site west of Jerusalem. Nehemiah would have been unprotected there.

- *plotting to revolt...become their king*: Those who opposed rebuilding the temple used similar tactics (see {{Ezra 4:1-24|Ezra 4}}). 

- At times in Israel's history, prophets helped establish a new king (compare {{1 Samuel 9:16|1 Samuel 9:16}}; {{2 Kings 9:1-37|2 Kings 9}}).
A good leader does not run from danger but stands as an example for their people.

*in fifty-two days*: Everyone understood that God's help made this success possible (see also {{Nehemiah 1:11|Nehemiah 1:11}}; {{Nehemiah 2:8|2:8}}, {{Nehemiah 2:18|18}}, {{Nehemiah 2:20|20}}; {{Nehemiah 4:15|4:15}}, {{Nehemiah 4:20|20}}).

- *the wall had been rebuilt*: The dedication of the wall is described in {{Nehemiah 12:27-34|Nehemiah 12:27–34}}. 

- The Levites typically helped care for the temple area and guarded its gates.

*a faithful man who feared God*: He showed two leadership traits that Nehemiah and God valued (see also {{Nehemiah 5:9|Nehemiah 5:9}}, {{Nehemiah 5:15|15}}; {{Daniel 6:4|Daniel 6:4}}; {{Luke 16:10-12|Luke 16:10–12}}; {{1 Peter 5:12|1 Peter 5:12}}).

The gatekeepers were meant to close the gates in the afternoon when people rested and were not ready to defend the city. In other texts, similar language describes the hottest part of the day when people go inside ({{Genesis 18:1|Genesis 18:1}}; {{2 Samuel 4:5|2 Samuel 4:5}}).

Most people lived in the countryside near their fields, so Jerusalem's population was small. A registration would likely encourage more people to settle in and near Jerusalem ({{Nehemiah 7:73|Nehemiah 7:73}}).

Not many people lived in Jerusalem in Nehemiah’s time. Most Jews who returned from Babylon lived in towns throughout Judah. The book of Nehemiah records times when they all gathered in Jerusalem.

They gathered for the Feast of Booths and to hear the Law of Moses read out loud. Ezra and the Levites read the law and explained it to the entire community. This included men, women and children.

This was a time of sadness as well as joy. Because God’s laws were explained to them, the people understood the Mount Sinai covenant. This meant that they understood the ways they hadn’t been faithful to God’s covenant. They were very sad about this. But Nehemiah encouraged them to celebrate the feast with joy. He reminded them that the joy of the Lord made them strong.

*the exiles...returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town*: These lists were incomplete (the individual numbers do not match the total in {{Nehemiah 7:66|Nehemiah 7:66}}), but they were the best records available to verify Jewish identity.

*accompanied by*: Sheshbazzar (see {{Ezra 1:8|Ezra 1:8}}) is not mentioned here and in {{Ezra 2:2|Ezra 2:2}}. This suggests both lists were made after the people settled in their towns and after Sheshbazzar died.

*the descendants of*: This list is similar to the one in {{Ezra 2:3-35|Ezra 2:3–35}}, but there are some differences in names and family sizes. People were listed by family ({{Nehemiah 7:8-25|Nehemiah 7:8–25}}) and by the town where they settled ({{Nehemiah 7:26-38|7:26–38}}). Most of these towns were north of Jerusalem.
Nehemiah wanted to ensure that only true priests and Levites served in God's temple.

The descendants of Solomon’s servants likely helped the Levites by carrying wood or sweeping the floor (see {{Ezra 2:55-58|Ezra 2:55–58}}). They might have been Gibeonites (see {{Joshua 9:23-27|Joshua 9:23–27}}; {{1 Chronicles 9:35-44|1 Chronicles 9:35–44}}) or war captives (see {{Numbers 31:30-47|Numbers 31:30–47}}).
*they could not prove that their families were descended from Israel*: They had no family records.
*Urim and Thummim*: See study notes on Exodus 28:30 and Leviticus 8:8.
The total number 42,360 matches {{Ezra 2:64|Ezra 2:64}}, but the family numbers add up to only 31,089. The family numbers might not include young children, or the list might be incomplete.

Some family leaders gave gifts, following their ancestors' traditions when building sacred structures ({{Exodus 25:2-7|Exodus 25:2–7}}; {{Exodus 35:4-9|35:4–9}}; {{2 Kings 12:1-21|2 Kings 12:1–21}}). This money added to gifts from Israelites who remained in Babylon ({{Ezra 1:6|Ezra 1:6}}) and from the Persian kings ({{Ezra 6:8|Ezra 6:8}}).
*the Israelites...in their own towns*: Each family settled in their ancestral towns throughout Israel, where their ancestors lived before the Exile.

This section, possibly from Ezra’s personal memoirs, explains how Ezra’s teaching of God’s law renewed the people's commitment to serve God and follow his instructions. Spiritual revival occurred alongside the civic work of Ezra and Nehemiah.

The Water Gate was in the middle of Jerusalem's eastern wall, south of the temple and east of the palace ruins ({{Nehemiah 3:26|Nehemiah 3:26}}; {{Nehemiah 12:37|12:37}}). There was a lot of open space, ensuring everyone could gather there.

*On the first day of the seventh month*: The people gathered to celebrate the Feast of Trumpets ({{Leviticus 23:24-25|Leviticus 23:24–25}}), marking the start of a new year in the calendar from after the exile in Babylon.

- The time from early morning until noon allowed about six hours for reading and interpreting ({{Nehemiah 8:7-8|Nehemiah 8:7–8}}). 

- *understand* (see also {{Nehemiah 8:2|Nehemiah 8:2}}, {{Nehemiah 8:8|8}}, {{Nehemiah 8:12|12}}): This was more than a ritual reading of the law. It included explanations, insights, and applications.
These thirteen people were likely community leaders. Some may have helped Ezra roll the scroll while he read.
The people stood up to show respect for God's word ({{Job 29:8|Job 29:8}}). They likely stood the entire time Ezra read.

- *Ezra blessed the LORD*: See also {{Nehemiah 1:5|Nehemiah 1:5}}; {{Nehemiah 9:32|9:32}}; {{Deuteronomy 10:17|Deuteronomy 10:17}}; {{Jeremiah 32:18|Jeremiah 32:18}}; {{Daniel 9:4|Daniel 9:4}}. 

- *Amen!* This is a statement of agreement (see {{Nehemiah 5:13|Nehemiah 5:13}}). Lifting hands ({{Psalm 28:2|Psalm 28:2}}) and bowing in humble worship showed reverence for God and submission to his word.

The Levites were responsible for teaching people God’s word ({{Deuteronomy 33:10|Deuteronomy 33:10}}; {{Malachi 2:5-6|Malachi 2:5–6}}). They likely explained the Hebrew Scriptures to smaller groups in Aramaic. Most people spoke Aramaic, the language of Babylon, instead of Hebrew as their first language. Jewish leaders later translated large parts of the Hebrew Bible into Aramaic, so people could hear and study the Bible in a language they understood.

- *Ezra the priest and scribe*: See study note on Ezra 7:6.

- *This day is holy to the LORD your God. Do not mourn or weep*: God moved the people's hearts, leading them to regret not following his laws. While weeping is a suitable reaction to sin (see {{Ezekiel 9:4|Ezekiel 9:4}}; {{Luke 6:21|Luke 6:21}}), Ezra and Nehemiah urged the people to celebrate what God had done. This New Year's festival was meant to be joyful ({{Numbers 29:1-6|Numbers 29:1–6}}), and weeping would have ruined the day's spirit.

- People ate rich foods like meat only on special occasions. 

- Sweet drinks meant unfermented juice, unlike the vinegar common laborers drank (see {{Ruth 2:14|Ruth 2:14}}). 

- It is good to share with those in need (see {{Deuteronomy 15:11|Deuteronomy 15:11}}; {{Job 29:16|Job 29:16}}; {{Proverbs 31:20|Proverbs 31:20}}; {{Matthew 6:2-3|Matthew 6:2–3}}; {{Acts 4:34-35|Acts 4:34–35}}).

*to make booths*: The Feast of Tabernacles commemorated when the people of Israel lived in tents during their journey through the wilderness ({{Leviticus 23:33-43|Leviticus 23:33–43}}; see also {{Numbers 29:12-39|Numbers 29:12–39}}; {{Deuteronomy 16:13-15|Deuteronomy 16:13–15}}).
The Ephraim Gate was likely on the north side of Jerusalem, facing the land of the tribe of Ephraim (see {{Nehemiah 12:39|Nehemiah 12:39}}).

*From the days of Joshua*: Israel had celebrated this festival many times ({{1 Kings 8:2|1 Kings 8:2}}; {{2 Kings 23:22|2 Kings 23:22}}; {{2 Chronicles 7:8-10|2 Chronicles 7:8–10}}; {{2 Chronicles 30:26|30:26}}; {{2 Chronicles 35:18|35:18}}; {{Ezra 3:4|Ezra 3:4}}), but this was a special celebration.

*Ezra read from the Book of the Law of God*: The law was read every seven years at the Feast of Booths ({{Deuteronomy 31:10-12|Deuteronomy 31:10–12}}). This reminded the people of the covenant rules and God's past acts of kindness.

The time for the people to show their sadness came after the Feast of Booths. The people gathered to admit all their sins out loud to God. They did this while they worshipped and praised God.

As they prayed, the Jews remembered God’s work among them. All the stories mentioned in the prayer are recorded in other books of the Bible. They are recorded in the books from Genesis through 2 Chronicles.

The Jews remembered when God told Abraham to move from Babylon to Canaan. They remembered how God had been faithful to them since then. They recognised that God is a gracious God. He had always been so good to them.

They also admitted all the ways that they had been proud and stubborn. Over and over God’s people had said no to him and they had chosen to do evil. They were very sorry about this and they repented. They were suffering. They longed for God to save them from being slaves of the Persian government.

So they once again committed to being faithful to the Mount Sinai covenant. This included men, women and children who were old enough to understand. They all agreed to follow God’s laws. They agreed not to join the families of people who worshipped false gods. They agreed to rest on the Sabbath day. They agreed to give the first share of their crops and a tenth of everything. They would give these to support the Levites and to take care of the temple.

*Those of Israelite descent separated themselves from all the foreigners, and they stood and confessed their sins*: This might refer to the issue of intermarriage with foreigners, as described in {{Ezra 9:1-10:44|Ezra 9–10}}.
They admitted their sins after listening to God's word (compare {{Nehemiah 8:1-9|Nehemiah 8:1–9}}, {{Nehemiah 8:13-14|13–14}}, {{Nehemiah 8:18|18}}).

The Levites' prayer praised God for his great reputation and his unique divinity. They acknowledged his creation of the universe and his care for life on earth. Angels worship him. Focusing on God helped Israel understand their current situation better.

This lengthy prayer admits the nation's sins and praises God for his compassion throughout history (compare {{Psalm 105:1-106:48|Psalms 105–106}}; {{Psalm 135:1-136:26|135–136}}). It encouraged listeners to admit their own unfaithfulness and ask God for compassion and forgiveness.

God's actions with Abram—calling him ({{Genesis 12:1-3|Genesis 12:1–3}}; {{Genesis 15:7|15:7}}), giving him a new name and identity ({{Genesis 17:5|Genesis 17:5}}), making a covenant with him ({{Genesis 15:6-21|Genesis 15:6–21}}; {{Genesis 17:4-5|17:4–5}}), and fulfilling his promises of land and descendants ({{Genesis 15:18-21|Genesis 15:18–21}})—showed God's faithfulness and inspired confidence in God's future actions.

God noticed his people's suffering under foreign rule ({{Exodus 2:23-25|Exodus 2:23–25}}; {{Exodus 3:7|3:7}}; {{Exodus 14:10-14|14:10–14}}), similar to their current situation ({{Nehemiah 9:32-37|Nehemiah 9:32–37}}).

*You made a name for Yourself*: In the Exodus, God showed his power with plagues, parting the sea, and defeating the proud Egyptian army ({{Exodus 15:5|Exodus 15:5}}, {{Exodus 15:9-10|9–10}}, {{Exodus 15:19|19}}).

This prayer reminded the people of God's miraculous guidance of Israel in the wilderness ({{Exodus 13:21-22|Exodus 13:21–22}}), his personal appearance at Mount Sinai to reveal his covenant laws through Moses (see {{Exodus 19:1-20:26|Exodus 19–20}}), and his faithfulness in providing bread and water (see {{Exodus 16:4|Exodus 16:4}}; {{Exodus 17:1-6|17:1–6}}). Despite all of that, Israel's ancestors were proud and stubborn and refused to obey (see {{Exodus 32:1-35|Exodus 32}}; {{Numbers 14:4|Numbers 14:4}}). Yet in his grace, God remained faithful and compassionate (see {{Exodus 34:6|Exodus 34:6}}) and provided his spirit to guide and teach them (compare {{Exodus 33:2|Exodus 33:2}}; {{Numbers 11:17|Numbers 11:17}}).

- Compare {{Deuteronomy 6:10-11|Deuteronomy 6:10–11}}; {{Deuteronomy 8:6-10|8:6–10}}. 

- *they ate and were filled; they grew fat*: Prosperity included spiritual danger (see {{Deuteronomy 8:11-20|Deuteronomy 8:11–20}}).
The prayer describes the events in the book of Judges (see {{Judges 2:11-23|Judges 2:11–23}}).

The people did not learn from the mistakes made during the time of the judges ({{Nehemiah 9:26-27|Nehemiah 9:26–27}}). The same pattern of disobedience appeared during the monarchy (compare {{2 Kings 17:1-41|2 Kings 17}}). Despite the nation's ongoing disobedience ({{Nehemiah 9:29|Nehemiah 9:29}}), God remained steadfast in his love, patience, compassion, and guidance through the spirit and the prophets.

The prayer now addresses the current situation, asking the great God—who has unfailing love—for ongoing love and mercy for his people in their difficult times ({{Nehemiah 9:32|Nehemiah 9:32}}). The leaders acknowledged God's justice in punishing them for their sins ({{Nehemiah 9:33-35|Nehemiah 9:33–35}}), and they expressed sorrow over their enslavement by the Persians ({{Nehemiah 9:36-37|9:36–37}}).
*we make a binding agreement, putting it in writing*: These actions shows a serious commitment to the agreement. The sealed document was legally binding.

The people, embracing the prayer, renewed their dedication to God and his word. They signed their names to show their commitment ({{Nehemiah 9:38-10:27|Nehemiah 9:38–10:27}}) and took an oath to follow the covenant ({{Nehemiah 10:28-39|10:28–39}}).

The list of eighty-four names included: 

- The governor, Nehemiah ({{Nehemiah 10:1|Nehemiah 10:1}})

- A group of priests ({{Nehemiah 10:2-8|Nehemiah 10:2–8}}; compare {{Nehemiah 12:1-7|12:1–7}})

- Levites ({{Nehemiah 10:9-13|Nehemiah 10:9–13}}; compare {{Nehemiah 9:4-5|9:4–5}}; {{Nehemiah 12:8-9|12:8–9}})

- Leaders ({{Nehemiah 10:14-27|Nehemiah 10:14–27}}; compare {{Nehemiah 3:4-31|3:4–31}})
*who had separated themselves from the people of the land*: See {{Nehemiah 9:2|Nehemiah 9:2}}; compare with {{Ezra 9:1-10:44|Ezra 9–10}}.
*sworn oath to follow the Law of God*: Compare {{Leviticus 26:14-35|Leviticus 26:14–35}} and {{Deuteronomy 28:15-62|Deuteronomy 28:15–62}}.

The community had broadly committed to following the law of Moses. However, they focused on specific issues. These issues involved keeping the community pure and ensuring proper worship at the temple.

- Stopping trade on the Sabbath was important for keeping the covenant (compare {{Nehemiah 13:15-22|Nehemiah 13:15–22}}; see {{Exodus 16:29|Exodus 16:29}}; {{Exodus 20:8-11|20:8–11}}; {{Exodus 31:15|31:15}}; {{Numbers 15:32-36|Numbers 15:32–36}}; {{Amos 8:5|Amos 8:5}}). 

- *Every seventh year*: See {{Exodus 23:10-11|Exodus 23:10–11}}; {{Leviticus 25:2-7|Leviticus 25:2–7}}; {{Deuteronomy 15:1-3|Deuteronomy 15:1–3}}.

- *the showbread*: See {{Leviticus 24:5-9|Leviticus 24:5–9}}; {{Numbers 28:1-8|Numbers 28:1–8}}. 

- *for all the duties*: The annual tax money allowed priests to buy animals for daily sacrifices and maintain the temple complex (compare {{2 Kings 12:11-12|2 Kings 12:11–12}}; see also {{Exodus 30:11-16|Exodus 30:11–16}}).

The fire on the altar burned constantly ({{Leviticus 6:12|Leviticus 6:12}}), so it required a lot of wood. The Gibeonites supplied it earlier ({{Joshua 9:27|Joshua 9:27}}), but now everyone shared the responsibility.

Community offerings provided food for the priests and Levites, who had no farmland and could not support themselves. These provisions included: 

- The first part of every harvest (see {{Exodus 23:19|Exodus 23:19}}; {{Exodus 34:26|34:26}}; {{Numbers 18:12-13|Numbers 18:12–13}}; {{Deuteronomy 26:1-11|Deuteronomy 26:1–11}})

- Redemption money of five shekels for the oldest sons and the firstborn of all herds and flocks (see {{Exodus 13:13|Exodus 13:13}}; {{Exodus 34:20|34:20}}; {{Numbers 18:15-17|Numbers 18:15–17}})

- A tenth of everything (see {{Numbers 18:21-24|Numbers 18:21–24}}; {{Deuteronomy 14:22-29|Deuteronomy 14:22–29}})
The Levites gathered tithes in all the rural towns and sent one-tenth of that collection to the temple in Jerusalem (see {{Numbers 18:25-32|Numbers 18:25–32}}).
Sacred lots were likely the Urim and Thummim ({{Nehemiah 10:34|Nehemiah 10:34}}; {{Joshua 7:14|Joshua 7:14}}, {{Joshua 7:16-18|16–18}}; {{Joshua 14:2|14:2}}).

The story goes back to the topic of bringing people back to live in the safe city of Jerusalem (see {{Nehemiah 7:1-5|Nehemiah 7:1–5}}). The list of names is similar to the one in {{1 Chronicles 9:2-17|1 Chronicles 9:2–17}}.

The book of Nehemiah records one more time when Jews throughout Judah gathered in Jerusalem. They gathered to set apart the wall that had been built around the city.

Ezra and other priests and Levites were there. They made themselves, the people, the wall and the gates pure and clean. Being pure and clean was necessary because God is holy and God was present with them.

The Levites and priests celebrated by marching, playing music, singing and offering sacrifices. Those who played instruments followed the instructions David had given when he was king. This showed that they worshipped God faithfully the way their people from long ago had.

The men, women and children who had gathered were full of joy. The joyful noise they made could be heard from far away. There were many reasons to be happy. God had brought his people back from exile. They had built a second temple and worshipped God there. They were living according to the Law of Moses in the Mount Sinai covenant.

Jerusalem was full of people because many people and leaders agreed to live there. Jerusalem had a strong wall around it again. Earlier in the book of Nehemiah the people had been ashamed. Now they were glad.
Perez was a son of Judah ({{Genesis 38:29|Genesis 38:29}}).

Outside the temple, the work likely involved collecting tithes from people and managing them in storehouses ({{Nehemiah 10:37-39|Nehemiah 10:37–39}}; see also {{1 Chronicles 26:29|1 Chronicles 26:29}}).

*the son of Asaph*: David selected Asaph and his sons to create music for temple worship ({{1 Chronicles 25:1-8|1 Chronicles 25:1–8}}). Asaph's descendants resumed this role when the new temple was built.
The hill of Ophel was high ground just south of the temple ({{Nehemiah 3:26|Nehemiah 3:26}}). It was a perfect place for housing temple workers.
The royal adviser told the king about events in Jerusalem and informed Jewish officials about the king's management of Persian policies.

*from Beersheba all the way to the Valley of Hinnom*: Earlier descriptions of where people settled focused on areas north of Jerusalem ({{Nehemiah 3:1-32|Nehemiah 3}}; {{Nehemiah 11:31-36|11:31–36}}). This list ({{Nehemiah 11:25-30|Nehemiah 11:25–30}}) shows the expansion of places where Jewish people lived as they returned to many of their towns from before the exile, both north and south of Jerusalem.

*priests and Levites who went up with Zerubbabel...with Jeshua*: See {{Ezra 1:1-5|Ezra 1:1–5}}. Only those who could prove their priestly lineage could serve at the temple. Therefore, maintaining an accurate genealogical record of these families was important.

These lists of priests and Levites include those who originally returned from exile with Zerubbabel ({{Nehemiah 12:1-9|Nehemiah 12:1–9}}), a chronological list of high priests ({{Nehemiah 12:10-11|12:10–11}}), and the priests and Levites who served during Joiakim's time, the high priest during Nehemiah and Ezra's era ({{Nehemiah 12:12-26|12:12–26}}).

- *leaders of the priests*: Compare {{Ezra 2:36-39|Ezra 2:36–39}}. 

- Jeshua was the high priest in Jerusalem when the people returned from captivity shortly after 538 BC ({{Ezra 2:2|Ezra 2:2}}; {{Ezra 3:2|3:2}}, {{Ezra 3:8|8}}; {{Ezra 4:3|4:3}}). He continued serving in 520 BC when Haggai and Zechariah encouraged the people to complete the temple ({{Ezra 5:1|Ezra 5:1}}; {{Haggai 1:1|Haggai 1:1}}; {{Zechariah 3:1|Zechariah 3:1}}).
*their associates, stood across*: To perform antiphonal singing (a call-and-response style) as described in {{Nehemiah 12:24|Nehemiah 12:24}}and {{Ezra 3:1-11|Ezra 3:1–11}}.

- Joiakim likely served during the early years of Ezra's service. 

- Eliashib and Joiada served during Nehemiah's time ({{Nehemiah 3:1|Nehemiah 3:1}}; {{Nehemiah 13:4|13:4}}, {{Nehemiah 13:28|28}}). 

- *Jonathan*: An Aramaic papyrus document from a Jewish colony in Elephantine, Egypt (around 410 BC). Josephus (*Antiquities* 11.5.4, AD 93) also mentions Jonathan serving after Nehemiah's time.

This list was likely compiled when Joiakim was the high priest ({{Nehemiah 12:12|Nehemiah 12:12}}) to confirm the legitimacy of the priests and Levites in office. Except for the omission of Hattush (see {{Nehemiah 12:2|Nehemiah 12:2}}), this list includes the same names as {{Nehemiah 12:1-7|Nehemiah 12:1–7}}.

- Since few Levites had returned to live in Jerusalem (see {{Ezra 2:40-42|Ezra 2:40–42}}; {{Ezra 8:15-19|8:15–19}}), leaders recruited all Levites throughout the land to form two impressive choirs and orchestras. 

- Netophathites came from near Bethlehem ({{1 Chronicles 2:54|1 Chronicles 2:54}}). 

- Beth-gilgal was near Jericho. 

- Geba and Azmaveth were in the territory of Benjamin.
The dedication of the new wall likely occurred soon after it was finished ({{Nehemiah 6:15-19|Nehemiah 6:15–19}}). This account likely came from Nehemiah’s personal writings.
The dedication ceremony required the priests and Levites to be purified and ready to enter the temple area (see {{Exodus 19:10|Exodus 19:10}}; {{Numbers 8:5-7|Numbers 8:5–7}}).

The impressive march moved south along the top of the wall to the Dung Gate at the city's southern end ({{Nehemiah 3:13-14|Nehemiah 3:13–14}}). Then the procession went north on the wall along the east side of the city, past the ruins of the house of David, and up to the Water Gate ({{Nehemiah 3:26|Nehemiah 3:26}}; {{Nehemiah 8:1|8:1}}) near the temple.

Long, slender, metal trumpets were played for joyful celebrations ({{1 Chronicles 13:8|1 Chronicles 13:8}}; {{1 Chronicles 15:23|15:23}}; {{1 Chronicles 16:6|16:6}}, {{1 Chronicles 16:42|42}}; {{Ezra 3:10|Ezra 3:10}}) by Asaph's descendants.

- The second choir went north along the western wall, passing: 

- The Broad Wall ({{Nehemiah 3:8|Nehemiah 3:8}})

- The Old City Gate ({{Nehemiah 3:6|Nehemiah 3:6}})

- The Fish Gate ({{Nehemiah 3:3|Nehemiah 3:3}})

They continued along the northern side of the wall until they reached the* Sheep Gate* ({{Nehemiah 3:1|Nehemiah 3:1}}) at the northeast corner of the temple. 

- The Guard Gate might be the* Inspection Gate *({{Nehemiah 3:31|Nehemiah 3:31}}).

This community celebration included everyone. God was the true source of their great joy because his power helped them rebuild the walls. {{Psalm 147:1-20|Psalm 147}} might have been written for this occasion.

On the day of the wall's dedication ({{Nehemiah 12:44|Nehemiah 12:44}}; {{Nehemiah 13:1|13:1}}), men were appointed to manage the tithes and gifts for the priests and Levites' needs. Their duties included collecting people's gifts for the priests and Levites ({{Nehemiah 10:32-39|Nehemiah 10:32–39}}; see also {{Exodus 30:11-16|Exodus 30:11–16}}; {{Exodus 38:25-26|38:25–26}}), performing services for God (probably sacrifices; see {{Leviticus 1:1-5:19|Leviticus 1–5}}), and overseeing the purification of unclean people. They also purified pans, knives, and clothing used in temple worship as described in {{Leviticus 11:1-15:33|Leviticus 11–15}} (see also {{1 Chronicles 23:28|1 Chronicles 23:28}}).

For some time the priests, Levites and people followed the Law of Moses carefully. The priests and Levites did their duties like they did when David and Solomon were kings. The Jews stopped allowing outsiders who didn’t worship God to be part of the community.

This didn’t mean that no Ammonite or Moabite could ever be part of God’s people. Some of David’s mighty warriors had been from Ammon and Moab (1 Chronicles 11:26–47). It meant that those who worshipped false gods couldn’t be full members of the community.

But then the priests, Levites and people stopped doing what they had agreed to do. The people stopped giving to the priests and Levites a tenth of what they owned. This led to the Levites stopping their work in the temple. A priest allowed Tobiah to use a room in the temple for his own work. Tobiah was an Ammonite who wasn’t fully committed to God.

Jewish men in Judah married women who didn’t worship God. This meant that they didn’t teach their children to worship only God. And the Jews started working, buying, selling and trading on the Sabbath day.

All these things happened after Nehemiah returned to Susa to continue serving Artaxerxes. These things showed that God’s people were once again acting like the people groups around them. They weren’t living as a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. Nehemiah had worked very hard to help them live the way God wanted them to. But he couldn’t force them to love God and serve God with their whole heart.

David gave instructions for organizing the music at the temple ({{1 Chronicles 23:1-26:32|1 Chronicles 23–26}}). He put Asaph, along with Heman and Jeduthun, in charge of the music ({{1 Chronicles 25:2-5|1 Chronicles 25:2–5}}).

From the time the first people returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel in 538 BC ({{Ezra 3:1|Ezra 3:1}}) until Nehemiah's time around 445 BC, Israelites provided food for temple workers. Most Levites lived in cities across the country. They collected a tithe and brought a tenth of it to the temple in Jerusalem to support its ministry (see {{Nehemiah 10:38-39|Nehemiah 10:38–39}}).

On the same day the temple workers were appointed ({{Nehemiah 12:44|Nehemiah 12:44}}), the text from {{Deuteronomy 23:3-6|Deuteronomy 23:3–6}} was read. It stated that no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God. Nehemiah later discovered ({{Nehemiah 13:4-14|Nehemiah 13:4–14}}) that people were no longer following these teachings.

Eliashib’s family married into the families of Sanballat ({{Nehemiah 13:28|Nehemiah 13:28}}) and Tobiah. These men were enemies of the Jewish community ({{Nehemiah 2:10|Nehemiah 2:10}}, {{Nehemiah 2:19|19}}; {{Nehemiah 4:1|4:1}}). Tobiah's use of the storeroom reduced space for storing tithes and gifts for temple workers (compare {{Nehemiah 10:39|Nehemiah 10:39}}; {{Nehemiah 13:10-12|13:10–12}}; {{2 Chronicles 31:11|2 Chronicles 31:11}}) and limited space for supplies needed for regular worship at the temple ({{Leviticus 2:1-16|Leviticus 2}}).

Eliashib the priest (see {{Nehemiah 12:10|Nehemiah 12:10}}, {{Nehemiah 12:22|22}}; {{Nehemiah 13:28|13:28}}) had stopped excluding the Ammonites and Moabites ({{Nehemiah 13:1|13:1}}). The people also stopped giving their tithes to the Levites ({{Nehemiah 13:10-12|Nehemiah 13:10–12}}). Nehemiah corrected these issues.

Nehemiah went back to Persia after serving in Jerusalem for twelve years, from 445 to 433 BC. The text does not specify how long he stayed in Persia, but it was likely no more than a year or two. When he returned to Jerusalem, he discovered Tobiah living in the temple storeroom ({{Nehemiah 13:1-5|Nehemiah 13:1–5}}).

- *I was greatly displeased...I ordered*: When people rejected God's instructions, Nehemiah spoke up. 

- Everything related to the temple had to be purified and dedicated to God. This included: 

- The clothes that the priests and Levites wore ({{Exodus 29:1-46|Exodus 29}})

- The priests themselves ({{Leviticus 8:1-9:24|Leviticus 8–9}})

- The temple building and altars ({{Leviticus 16:15-33|Leviticus 16:15–33}})

- All the holy items ({{1 Chronicles 23:28|1 Chronicles 23:28}})

They were all purified (compare {{2 Chronicles 29:5|2 Chronicles 29:5}}, {{2 Chronicles 29:15-19|15–19}}).

Because Tobiah used the storeroom, there was no space to store tithes for feeding the Levites and temple singers ({{Numbers 18:21-24|Numbers 18:21–24}}; see {{Nehemiah 12:44|Nehemiah 12:44}}, {{Nehemiah 12:47|47}}). They had to farm outside Jerusalem ({{Nehemiah 12:28-29|Nehemiah 12:28–29}}) to support themselves and could not serve in the temple.

Nehemiah asked God to remember his good deeds and not abandon him when he needed help. He likely faced opposition from those he corrected. See similar mentions in {{Nehemiah 13:22|Nehemiah 13:22}}, {{Nehemiah 13:29|29}}, {{Nehemiah 13:31|31}}.
People were to stop working on the Sabbath to keep it holy ({{Exodus 20:8-11|Exodus 20:8–11}}; {{Exodus 31:14-17|31:14–17}}; {{Exodus 35:2-3|35:2–3}}; {{Jeremiah 17:19-27|Jeremiah 17:19–27}}).

Nehemiah made two more changes to bring back correct Sabbath observance ({{Nehemiah 13:15-22|Nehemiah 13:15–22}}) and correct marriage practices ({{Nehemiah 13:23-31|13:23–31}}). These two sections follow a similar pattern: Nehemiah found a problem, fixed it, and then asked God for a blessing.
The Sabbath starts at sunset on Friday evening and ends at sunset on Saturday evening.
*show me mercy*: Nehemiah's prayer suggests he felt the pressure of this unpopular decision. He knew God's unfailing love, not his popularity, would sustain him.

The earlier marriage reforms ({{Nehemiah 9:2|Nehemiah 9:2}}; {{Nehemiah 10:28|10:28}}; {{Ezra 9:1-10:44|Ezra 9:1–10:44}}) did not last. The children could not speak Hebrew, the language of Judah. This was disastrous because they could not read or understand the Scriptures.

- Nehemiah cursed them because the parents avoided Hebrew and did not teach their children the language of the Hebrew Bible. A curse asked God to remove his blessing from people. 

- *I beat some of these men and pulled out their hair*: Some men did not accept Nehemiah’s rebuke at first, so he made them swear in the name of God not to marry pagans.

King Solomon led the nation into sin through his foreign wives ({{1 Kings 11:1-43|1 Kings 11}}). If intermarriage with non-believers continued, the community would face the same downfall. Nehemiah would not allow that.

Even the family of the high priest, who were meant to be Israel’s spiritual leaders, participated in the sin of intermarriage with unbelieving foreigners (compare {{Leviticus 21:14|Leviticus 21:14}}). Nehemiah banished the offender, stripping him of status and removing his rights in the Jewish community.

*Remember them, O my God*: Many likely resented Nehemiah's strong stance against intermarriage in the high priest's family. He prayed for God's judgment on these spiritual leaders who defiled the priesthood.
These final verses summarize Nehemiah’s reform. Nehemiah ensured the people kept their promises. He held them accountable and did not accept half-hearted efforts.
